speaker: Kelsey Hightower
title: Kubernetes and retiring at the top with Kelsey Hightower
question: In software engineering, why is repeatedly using AI to regenerate common code blocks a structural mistake even when generation is fast?
guest: There's this mindset where people really think it makes sense to do inference every single time. When a human writes a piece of code—say authenticating to an endpoint—you look up the documentation and write it once. If you have to do it twice, it becomes a function you call multiple times in the codebase. If you do it five to ten times, it becomes a library imported across multiple apps, and eventually those solved patterns get baked into the framework, the operating system, or even offloaded to hardware. That has been the loop software engineers go through for a long time because there is no need to re-derive a solved problem from scratch. Generative AI should be no different. If you find yourself generating the same blocks of code over and over, even though it feels fast or convenient, it is still insane—you're just copying the same block everywhere, and we already know where that leads.

points.core: Healthy engineering progressively compresses repeated code into shared reusable abstractions.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Because the cost of code was never mainly in typing it; it lies in owning it afterward. Regenerating a common block each time you need it produces duplication rather than abstraction, and fast generation only makes the duplication accumulate faster.

Each regenerated copy is a separate piece of code that must be read, reviewed, tested, and maintained on its own. Since generation is non-deterministic, the copies also drift subtly, handling edge cases, errors, and naming differently, so the system has no single, authoritative behavior. When a bug or security flaw is found, or requirements change, there is no one place to fix it: you must hunt down every variant, and you will likely miss some.

A shared function, module, or library inverts this. It is written once, tested once, and improved everywhere at the same time. It also gives the concept a name, which shrinks the codebase and the amount humans and AI tools must hold in context to reason about it.

In short, generation speed optimizes the cheap part, writing, while multiplying the expensive part: comprehension, verification, and change. This is the DRY principle, and AI doesn't repeal it.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: Repeatedly regenerating common code with AI optimizes for writing speed at the expense of system structure, destroying a codebase's single source of truth. Because the dominant cost of software is reading, testing, and evolving code rather than typing it, fast generation does not make duplication free. When shared logic is regenerated instead of consolidated into reusable abstractions, every instance becomes an independent maintenance liability. Worse than traditional copy-pasting, probabilistic models introduce subtle semantic drift, producing slight variations in validation, edge-case handling, naming, and error recovery across similar blocks. Engineers must review and test each variation separately, inflating cognitive load and expanding the bug and security surface. When requirements shift, an API changes, or a defect surfaces, teams cannot update one authoritative module; they must hunt down and reconcile dozens of slightly different implementations, inevitably missing some. Ultimately, frictionless generation masks design smells—removing the healthy pain of repetition that normally prompts engineers to build clean, composable boundaries and cohesive domain abstractions.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Generation cost was never the main cost. The expensive parts of code are reading, reviewing, testing, and maintaining it, and every regenerated copy adds to all of them. When AI writes a fresh version of the same logic in ten places, you don't get one abstraction. You get ten slightly different versions, each with its own edge cases, naming quirks, and possible bugs. That breaks DRY and spreads one concept across the codebase as duplication.

The structural problem shows up when things change. If a requirement shifts or a security flaw turns up, a shared function or library needs one fix. Scattered regenerated copies have to be found and patched one by one, and some will be missed. Because the variants differ a little, they also behave inconsistently, which makes them harder to test as a group and harder to reason about. Each copy has to be reviewed on its own too, so reviewers spend time re-checking code that should have been trusted once.

Repeated generation also skips the design step of naming a recurring pattern and giving it a single owner. Fast generation treats the symptom, which is typing effort. The fix is abstraction: shared modules, templates, or libraries.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: Fast generation only lowers the initial cost of writing code, whereas most of a software system's cost comes from reading, testing, debugging, and changing it over time. Repeatedly regenerating common code blocks bakes duplication directly into the architecture and destroys the single source of truth. Because AI outputs vary slightly across prompts and contexts, each regenerated copy tends to drift in subtle ways—handling edge cases, errors, or state differently. When a business rule changes or a security flaw is discovered, engineers can no longer fix one well-tested abstraction; they must hunt down and reconcile every divergent variant across the codebase, multiplying review overhead and the risk of inconsistent behavior. It also inflates the codebase's surface area, increasing cognitive load for both humans and future AI tools trying to navigate the system. In short, cheap code generation does not make code cheap to own; extracting shared, well-contracted abstractions remains essential to prevent compounding technical debt.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Fast generation lowers the cost of writing code, but every generated copy still has to be reviewed, tested, and maintained. If several copies implement the same rule, a bug fix or requirement change has to reach all of them. Small differences in what the AI generates can also make those copies behave inconsistently, especially in edge cases.

When the blocks serve the same purpose and should change together, put the shared logic in a function, component, or library. Then callers use one implementation, and a fix in that implementation reaches them all. AI can help build the abstraction, but generating another copy leaves the maintenance cost in place.

Fast generation makes code cheap to produce, but each copy still has to be understood, tested, and maintained. When several parts of a system implement the same rule independently, a bug fix or requirement change has to reach every copy. Even small differences can make the system behave inconsistently.

If those blocks are supposed to change together, put the shared behavior in a function, module, or library and have callers use it. Then one change can fix every caller, and the code makes their shared dependency explicit. The structural mistake is duplicating a decision that should have one source of truth.
